A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' study of benign overfitting in attention token selection. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive scientific revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments on attention dynamics, training/test losses, and theorem-condition diagnostics in Section 5 and Appendix I.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic experiments and experiments on six real datasets, including training losses and test accuracies in Table 2 and supplementary material in Appendix G.

M1.justification: v1 optimizes only the token p from zero while fixing an orthogonal query-key matrix W. v2 jointly optimizes W and p from Gaussian initialization (Section 3.4). This substantially changes the training procedure and dynamics, although the attention formula and cross-entropy objective are retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic noisy binary classification. v2 retains that coverage and adds MNIST, CIFAR-10, PneumoniaMNIST, BreastMNIST, AG-news, and TREC, extending evaluation to image recognition, medical classification, news topics, and question types. The theoretical multiclass discussion already existed in v1.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically compares the proposed procedure against competing methods. ViT and BERT are backbones for v2's experiments; its new Table 1 compares theoretical literature rather than evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Synthetic experiments change weak-signal strength from 0.2 to 0.1, learning rate from 1e-4 to 5e-3, initialization, and some dimension/signal settings. The loss heatmap changes from 20,000 to 1,000 iterations. New real-data protocols train final attention query-key weights for 2,000 epochs with label-noise rate 0.1 and training subsets ranging from 20 to 1,000 examples.

E4.justification: The empirical checks of v1's trajectory conditions, Equations 9 and 10, are removed with Figures 4 and 6. The dimension/signal sensitivity heatmap is revised, and v2 adds training-size sensitivity across six real datasets to investigate transitions between fitting regimes (Section 5, Table 2).

E5.justification: v1 mentions trials and training runs without explicit run counts or uncertainty estimates. v2 Table 2 newly reports means and standard deviations over three runs. This is a localized addition of uncertainty reporting, not evidence of increased repetitions for the retained synthetic experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds the six-dataset results in Table 2 and revises synthetic trajectories and loss heatmaps. For example, Figure 3's harmful-overfitting test accuracy changes from 0.91 at d=4500 to 0.87 at d=5000, alongside other setting changes, so this is not a same-setting decline. The old trajectory-condition diagnostic results are removed.

T1.justification: v1's existence construction and trajectory-conditional convergence results are replaced by finite-time, SNR-based benign and not-overfitting results. v2 introduces attention-gap definitions and staged inductive proofs in Appendices D–E, with substantially revised parameter and data assumptions, including isotropic noise, single relevant/confusing tokens, and constant-order sequence length. The multiclass appendix is adapted; the earlier fixed-head ETF lemma and formal harmful-overfitting proof are removed.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion shift from existence and conditional benign/harmful convergence to SNR-based guarantees for joint attention training. v2 adds delayed-generalization/grokking claims and real-data support as contributions. These materially redefine the paper's main results and scope.

C2.justification: v2 explains delayed generalization through slow signal learning and the exponential training-time term, adding a grokking interpretation absent from v1. Remark 4.2 discusses harmful behavior outside the guaranteed SNR regime. Section 5 also adds dataset-specific interpretations, including BreastMNIST's failure to overfit and AG-news results suggesting harmful overfitting.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's synthetic settings, v2 Appendix G.2 documents ViT/BERT configurations, disabled dropout, separate clean-data classifier-head training, subset sizes, image processing, and AdamW with learning-rate scheduling. These substantially expand reproducibility information for the new experiments. Both versions provide the same code-repository link.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through Table 1 and Appendix A, including comparisons with Jiang et al., Magen et al., and Sheen et al. It distinguishes label noise, token types, optimized parameters, and training horizons, and adds grokking literature. v1's broad first-study positioning is replaced by explicit differentiation from recent and concurrent attention work.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related-work emphasis is reordered, data/model subsections exchange positions, and the main-results narrative changes from existence/convergence/difficulties to a theorem followed by key techniques. The appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are redesigned or reorganized, including SNR annotations and changed noisy-sample panels. v2 adds theoretical-comparison, experimental-results, and dataset-detail tables. The old condition-diagnostic heatmaps disappear; the retained loss heatmap is redrawn as Figure 4 rather than constituting an entirely new analysis.

improvement.justification: Under revised assumptions, v2 addresses v1's central reliance on assumed attention trajectories with explicit SNR-based finite-time analysis and detailed staged proofs (Section 4, Appendices D–E). Real-data experiments, uncertainty reporting, and implementation details substantially strengthen empirical grounding. The narrower token/noise assumptions and loss of the formal harmful-overfitting branch limit the extension, but the more explicit convergence conditions and training-time analysis provide a substantial overall quality gain.
